bt67yj-p153363-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for distinction 44 and its first section, announcing the topic: whether the power to sin comes from God.

bt67yj-p153363-d1e122.summary: The paragraph frames the response to the distinction's first question — whether man or angel received the power to sin from God — announcing that the answer will proceed by three conclusions or parts, corresponding to a threefold sense in which 'power to sin' can be understood.
claims: The question of whether the power to sin comes from God requires disambiguating three distinct senses of 'power to sin' before it can be answered.
concepts: threefold division of a term (potentia peccandi)

bt67yj-p153363-d1e140.summary: The paragraph treats the first sense of 'power to sin': the natural power or faculty of the soul by which we act well or badly, chiefly the will, and the other faculties (intellect, sense, sensual appetite, locomotive power) that the will commands. This natural faculty is certainly from God, though it is less usually called 'power to sin' — Augustine instead calls it 'possibility' and teaches (On the Grace of Christ, ch. 17ff.) that it is from God.
claims: The natural faculty of the soul (will and the faculties it commands) by which one can act well or badly is certainly from God.
This natural faculty is better termed 'possibility' (following Augustine) than 'power to sin' in the strict sense.

bt67yj-p153363-d1e163.summary: The paragraph treats the second sense: 'power' or, more commonly, 'permission/authority to sin' (potestas peccandi), meaning an unimpeded faculty to carry a sin through to actual execution without hindrance. This too is from God, not only because the underlying natural faculty is from God, but because that a good or evil act can and does actually occur at a determinate time and place pertains to divine ordination. Scripture and the Fathers frequently attribute this sense of 'power to sin' to God: the devil could not tempt Job, nor deceive Achab, except by power received from God; Christ told Pilate his power to crucify him was given from above (John 19).
claims: The 'power' or 'authority' to actually carry out a sinful act unimpeded is from God, because the occurrence of the act at a given time and place falls under divine ordination.
Scripture attributes this authorizing sense of power over sinful acts to God in several episodes (Job, Achab, Pilate).
concepts: divine ordination of the occurrence of acts
scriptural instances of God authorizing evil agents' power

bt67yj-p153363-d1e207.summary: The paragraph extends and reinforces the second sense with further scriptural and patristic testimony: Scripture generally attributes to God the whole power that the impious wield against the pious (Hosea 13, Job 34, Christ's words on 'the power of darkness'). Augustine repeatedly teaches, citing Romans 13 ('there is no power except from God'), that the power to harm is never had except as given by God — malice supplies the desire, but only God's permission supplies the power — and cites this doctrine across many of his works (Enarrationes on Psalms 32, 56, 96; On the Nature of the Good; On Genesis to the Letter; To Simplician; On the Spirit and the Letter), as does Gregory the Great.
claims: Scripture generally attributes to God the power the wicked wield against the righteous, even when their malice is their own.
Augustine's consistent teaching, grounded in Romans 13, is that the capacity to actually inflict harm is granted only by God's permission, distinct from the evil desire itself, which is not from God.
This doctrine is confirmed across a wide range of Augustine's works and echoed by Gregory the Great.
concepts: distinction between evil desire and the power/permission to act on it

bt67yj-p153363-d1e268.summary: The paragraph treats the third sense: 'power to sin' taken as the power of failing or falling short of what is right and just, which in matters of morals can be called 'defectibility.' Because this is properly not a power but an impotence (just as being able to fall ill is properly not an ability but an inability), it is not from God but from the imperfection of the creature itself, which, having been made from nothing, has of itself the capacity to fail, sin, and be reduced to nothing. If this kind of potency were from God, the sin arising from it would also be from God, since the proper act belongs to the same source as the potency; Augustine (City of God XIV.13, XII.1) and others confirm that creatures' mutability and defectibility stem from their being made ex nihilo, not from their being made by God.
claims: Defectibility — the capacity to fail or fall short of the right — is properly an impotence, not a potency.
Defectibility is not from God but from the creature's own imperfection as something made from nothing.

If defectibility (and the sin arising from it) were from God, sin itself would be from God, since a potency and its proper act share the same source — which is unacceptable, so defectibility must be traced instead to the creature's origin ex nihilo.
concepts: defectibility (defectibilitas) as impotence rather than potency
creation ex nihilo as source of mutability
principle that potency and its proper act share a common source

bt67yj-p153363-d1e329.summary: A brief bibliographic-critical note observing that a divergent view is found in the letter to Demetrias (beginning 'Si summo ingenio'), transmitted among the letters of both Augustine and Jerome, but that this letter belongs to neither of them and is in fact authored by Pelagius, as can be shown by certain arguments drawn from Augustine.
claims: The letter to Demetrias, though transmitted under Augustine's or Jerome's name, is actually the work of Pelagius, contrary to the doctrine defended in this chapter.

bt67yj-p153363-d1e342.summary: The paragraph addresses a potentially conflicting Augustinian text (on Psalm 61), where God is said to have given men the power to do good and not to do evil: although this could be read in terms of the 'defectibility' sense just discussed, it is better understood as referring to some positive power whose proper act is precisely to do evil, since in that passage Augustine is arguing against the Genethliaci (astrologers) who claimed that men do evil under the compulsion of the stars.
claims: Augustine's statement on Psalm 61 about God giving the power to do good and avoid evil is better read as referring to a positive power to sin (the second sense), not to mere defectibility, given its polemical context against astrological determinism.

bt67yj-p153363.summary: Capitulum 1 answers the question of distinction 44 whether the power to sin comes from God by distinguishing three senses of 'power to sin': (1) the natural faculty of the soul (will and its subordinate powers), which is from God; (2) the unimpeded power or authority actually to carry out a sinful act, which is likewise from God insofar as the occurrence of any act at all falls under divine ordination and permission, richly attested in Scripture and especially Augustine; and (3) defectibility, the creature's capacity to fail or fall short of the right, which — being properly an impotence rather than a potency — is not from God but from the creature's own origin ex nihilo. The chapter closes by dismissing a spurious Augustinian/Hieronymian text (actually Pelagius's) and reconciling an apparently conflicting Augustinian passage by reading it in the second, positive sense of power.
claims: The power to sin must be disambiguated into three senses before the question of its divine origin can be answered.
The natural faculty of the soul and the unimpeded power actually to execute an act (including a sinful one) are both from God.
Defectibility — the capacity to fail or fall short of the right — is not from God, but arises from the creature's imperfection as something made from nothing.
The letter to Demetrias, sometimes attributed to Augustine or Jerome, is actually by Pelagius and represents a divergent, rejected view.
